newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress reaffirms vow to topple govt.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress reaffirms vow to topple govt.

text.p: India's political crisis deepened on Monday as the rebellious Congress party restated its determination to bring down Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority government.

The ruling United Front coalition faces a confidence vote in the lower house of the parliament on Friday, called by President Shankar Dayal Sharma after Congress president Sitaram Kesri withdrew its make-or-break support.
"It is highly unlikely that anything will happen before (Friday)," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told Reuters on Monday when asked what his party's next steps would be.
"Let the government fall first and then we will decide."
The United Front, whose members range from free traders to communists, has needed the support of 140 Congress lawmakers in the 542-member lower house of the parliament for its survival.
The United Front has 180 deputies in the house.
Kesri on Sunday made a strong verbal attack on Deve Gowda, threatening to scuttle ongoing informal talks between some senior United Front and Congress leaders to resolve the crisis.
Kesri's verbal attack is seen as an attempt to engineer a split in the 15-party government and woo some regional parties from the coalition over to Congress.
"They (Congress) made a disastrous miscalculation and want us (United Front) to pay the price," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy said on Monday.
The United Front stood solidly behind Deve Gowda, Reddy said, adding that Kesri's attack on Deve Gowda would boomerang.
"Congress will break up before April 10," he predicted.
Many politicians feel that the main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), the largest in the lower house with 162 members, will be the only gainer from the impasse.
"The party's intention is to vote out the government. It is not interested in a change of leadership in the United Front," The Times of India newspaper quoted BJP spokeswoman Sushma Swaraj as saying.
But BJP leaders said last week that the party was not in a position to form a stable government and favoured a mid-term poll, which opinion surveys suggest would benefit the party.
The BJP's national executive met in the Indian capital over the weekend.
Some Congress and United Front leaders said they expected informal talks between the leaders of the two parties would help thwart any BJP attempts to seize power.
"I am positive," a senior Congress leader, who asked not to be identified, said when asked about prospects for the talks.
"The country is not prepared for another round of elections and we should also stop a BJP-led government."
